# Orchestrating Agents with Workflows {#sec-workflows}

In the previous chapters, you learned how to deploy models, configure agents
with tools and memory, and fine-tune those agents for specialized tasks. A
single, well-tuned agent can carry a conversation, call an API, and synthesize
results, but it hits a ceiling quickly when a task requires distinct phases of
work, conditional logic, or human sign-off. That is where **Workflows** come in.

Workflows are Microsoft Foundry's visual orchestration layer. They let you
string together multiple agents, data transformations, branching logic, and
human checkpoints into a repeatable, auditable process, all without abandoning the
low-code builder that makes Foundry approachable. Think of a workflow as a
directed graph: nodes are actions (invoke an agent, set a variable, ask a
question), and edges encode order and conditions.

This chapter covers the three core orchestration patterns Foundry ships as
templates, walks through building a sequential pipeline from scratch, and then
digs into Power Fx, the formula language you will use any time you need more
than a straight-line flow.

::: {.callout-note}
Workflows are currently a UI-based, no-code/low-code feature. If you want to
manage workflow definitions as code, say, to version them in Git or
deploy them through a CI pipeline, see Foundry's VS Code extensions, which
surface the same YAML that backs the visual builder. The YAML view and the
visual view stay in sync; changes to one appear immediately in the other.
:::

## When to Reach for a Workflow

Not every multi-step task needs a workflow. If you can express the logic inside
a single agent's system prompt and tool calls, keep it there, the overhead of a
visual orchestration layer is rarely justified for a two-step chain.

Workflows earn their keep when you need at least one of the following:

**Multiple agents with distinct roles.** A triage agent that classifies an
incoming request, a retrieval agent that fetches relevant documents, and a
summarization agent that drafts the response each have a clear boundary of
responsibility. Stitching them in a single prompt muddies those boundaries and
makes debugging harder.

**Branching logic that belongs outside the model.** If your flow depends on
structured conditions, "if the customer tier is Enterprise, route to the
premium support agent; otherwise, route to the self-serve agent", encode that
logic in the workflow, not in a prompt. Prompts are not reliable control flow.

**Human checkpoints.** Approval gates, clarifying questions, and escalations all
require pausing execution and waiting for a person to respond. Workflows have a
dedicated node type for this pattern; there is no clean way to implement it
inside a single agent loop.

**Auditable, reusable pipelines.** Versioning is built into the workflow engine.
Every save creates a new, immutable version. That makes it straightforward to
roll back, compare runs across versions, and meet compliance requirements that
ask "what logic produced this output?"

## The Three Orchestration Patterns

Foundry provides three template patterns (@fig-patterns). You can start from a
blank canvas, but these templates cover the majority of real-world cases.

<!-- ![The three Foundry workflow orchestration patterns.](foundry_workflow_orchestration_patterns){#fig-patterns} -->

### Sequential

The simplest and most common pattern. Each agent receives the output of the
previous one and passes its result downstream. The order is fixed at design
time.

Sequential workflows are the right choice for **pipeline-style tasks**: ingest
→ enrich → validate → format → deliver. They are predictable, easy to
test step-by-step, and easy to explain to stakeholders.

Use this pattern when the stages of a task are well-defined and the output of
one stage is always the input to the next. If the routing between stages depends
on content or context, look at the group chat pattern instead.

### Group Chat

The group chat pattern introduces an **orchestrator agent** that routes control
to specialist agents dynamically, based on the conversation context or on
explicit rules. After a specialist responds, control returns to the orchestrator,
which decides the next step.

This is the right pattern for **escalation and handoff scenarios**: a general
intake agent that decides whether a request needs a legal reviewer, a compliance
checker, or a technical expert. It is also useful when you cannot enumerate all
routing paths at design time, the orchestrator's prompt or tools handle the
decision at runtime.

The trade-off is observability. A sequential workflow is trivially traceable;
the group chat pattern requires you to instrument the orchestrator carefully to
understand why control went where it did.

### Human in the Loop

This pattern inserts a pause node at any point in the workflow, Foundry halts
execution and waits for a human response before proceeding. The human's input is
then available as a variable to downstream nodes.

Common applications include:

- **Approval gates**: a workflow that drafts a contract and then pauses for a
  legal reviewer before sending it.
- **Ambiguity resolution**: an intake agent that surfaces a clarifying question
  to the user when confidence is low.
- **Exception handling**: a monitoring workflow that flags an anomaly and pages
  an on-call engineer.

Human-in-the-loop steps can be composed freely with the other patterns. A
sequential workflow might include one human approval gate; a group chat workflow
might escalate to a human as one of its routing paths.

## Building a Sequential Workflow

The best way to internalize how workflows are assembled is to build one. This
section walks through a concrete example: a three-agent pipeline that processes
a customer support ticket, enriches it with account data, and drafts a response.

### Creating the Workflow

Sign in to the Foundry portal and navigate to your project. On the upper-right
menu, select **Build**, then **Create new workflow > Sequential**. Foundry opens
the visual builder with a template containing placeholder agent nodes arranged
in a chain.

::: {.callout-important}
Foundry does not save workflows automatically. Get into the habit of selecting
**Save** after every meaningful change. The versioning system creates a new
immutable snapshot on each save, so saving frequently gives you fine-grained
rollback points.
:::

### Adding Nodes

Nodes are the building blocks of any workflow. Each node represents a single
action. To add a node, select the **+** icon in the workspace. The common node
types you will use most are:

- **Agent**: invokes a Foundry agent and passes it an input.
- **Ask a question**: prompts the user for input and stores the response as a
  named variable.
- **Send message**: pushes text output to the user.
- **If/else**: branches the flow based on a Power Fx condition.
- **For each**: iterates over a list.
- **Set variable**: stores or transforms a value using a Power Fx expression.

To reorder nodes, select the three dots on a node and choose **Move**. To
remove a node, select **Delete**. Both operations preserve the connections to
adjacent nodes where the topology still makes sense.

### Assigning Agents to Nodes

Select an agent node in the visualizer. A configuration panel opens on the
right. You have two options:

- **Existing agent**: search for any agent you have already created in this
  project. The search is live and scoped to the project.
- **New agent**: enter a name and description; Foundry creates a new agent
  scoped to this workflow. You can configure its model, system prompt, and tools
  inline without leaving the workflow builder.

For the support-ticket pipeline, you would configure three nodes:

1. **Classify**: a lightweight agent with a compact model (Haiku or GPT-4o-mini)
   that categorizes the ticket by type and priority.
2. **Enrich**: an agent with an HTTP tool call that fetches the customer's
   account tier and recent interactions from your CRM.
3. **Draft**: an agent with a richer model that composes the response, instructed
   to match tone to the tier and priority returned by the upstream nodes.

### Structured Output Between Nodes

When one agent's output needs to be consumed programmatically by the next node
— rather than passed as freeform text, configure it to emit a JSON schema.

In the agent configuration panel, select **Details**, then the parameter icon,
and set **Text format** to **JSON Schema**. Paste your schema into the **Add
response format** dialog. For the Classify agent, a minimal schema might look
like this:

```json
{
  "name": "ticket_classification",
  "schema": {
    "type": "object",
    "properties": {
      "category":  { "type": "string" },
      "priority":  { "type": "string", "enum": ["low", "medium", "high", "critical"] },
      "sentiment": { "type": "string", "enum": ["positive", "neutral", "negative"] }
    },
    "required": ["category", "priority", "sentiment"],
    "additionalProperties": false
  },
  "strict": true
}
```

After saving the schema, select **Action settings > Save output json_object /
json_schema as**, create a new variable (for example, `classification`), and
select **Done**. Downstream nodes can now reference `Local.classification` in
Power Fx expressions.

::: {.callout-warning}
Never include API keys, tokens, or passwords in JSON schemas, workflow
variables, or system prompts. These values appear in plaintext in workflow
version history and in run logs.
:::

### Running and Verifying the Workflow

Select **Run Workflow**. A chat panel opens. Send a sample ticket, for example,
"My invoice from last month is incorrect and I cannot reach anyone by phone" —
and watch the visualizer. Each node highlights as it executes; a green checkmark
indicates success, a red X indicates a failure with a log you can inspect.

After the run completes, verify three things:

1. Each node shows a green checkmark.
2. The chat panel shows the drafted response.
3. The `classification` variable contains the JSON you expect. (You can inspect
   saved variable values in the run log.)

If the Classify agent returns prose instead of JSON, confirm the schema is saved
and that the model you chose supports structured output. Some smaller models do
not reliably enforce schemas; GPT-4o and Claude 3.5 Sonnet are safe choices for
structured output tasks.

## Expressing Logic with Power Fx

Power Fx is the expression language that runs inside workflow nodes. If you have
used Excel formulas or Power Automate, the syntax will feel familiar. Power Fx
lets you construct conditions, transform strings, parse JSON, and route the
flow, all without writing Python or JavaScript.

### Variable Scoping

Every expression that references a variable needs a scope prefix:

- `Local.` for variables defined within this workflow (for example, user
  responses saved by an Ask-a-question node, or JSON output saved by an agent
  node).
- `System.` for runtime context provided by the platform (for example,
  `System.LastMessage.Text`, `System.User.Language`, or
  `System.Conversation.Id`).

Forgetting the prefix is the single most common Power Fx mistake. If you see a
"Name isn't valid" error, the prefix is almost certainly missing.

### Useful Formulas by Type

The table below maps data types to the Power Fx functions you will reach for
most often. This is not exhaustive. The full reference is available in
Microsoft's Power Fx documentation, but it covers 80% of workflow expression
needs.

| Type | Formulas you will use |
|------|----------------------|
| String | `Upper()`, `Lower()`, `Concat()`, `Len()`, `Text()`, `Find()`, `Substitute()` |
| Boolean | `If()`, `And()`, `Or()`, `Not()`, `Switch()` |
| Number | `Value()`, `Int()`, `Round()` |
| Record / Table | `ParseJSON()`, `JSON()`, `Filter()`, `ForAll()`, `First()`, `LookUp()` |
| Date / Time | `Now()`, `DateAdd()`, `DateDiff()`, `Text()` |
| Blank / Error | `IsBlank()`, `Coalesce()`, `IfError()` |

: Common Power Fx functions by data type. {#tbl-powerfx}

### Setting Variables

The most basic Power Fx use case is storing and transforming a value for
downstream use. Continuing the support-ticket example, suppose you want to
extract the `priority` field from the `classification` variable and store it as
a standalone string:
ParseJSON(Local.classification).priority

Wire this expression into a **Set variable** node, name the output
`ticket_priority`, and every subsequent node can branch on `Local.ticket_priority`
without needing to re-parse the JSON.

### Building If/Else Branches

Select the **+** icon and choose **If/else** to split the flow into conditional
branches. In the **Condition** box, type a Power Fx expression that evaluates to
a Boolean. The `System.` prefix unlocks autocomplete for all system variables.

For the support-ticket pipeline, a branch on priority might look like:
Local.ticket_priority = "critical"

Connect the `true` branch to a node that escalates to a human reviewer; connect
the `false` branch to the Draft agent. You can add additional `else if` branches
for intermediate priorities.

::: {.callout-tip}
**Type mismatch errors** are the other common Power Fx failure mode. If a
condition compares a number to a string, or if an agent node returns a JSON
field as a string that you then try to use as a number, wrap it in a conversion
function: `Value(ParseJSON(Local.classification).priority_score)` coerces a
numeric-looking string to an actual number.
:::

### A Complete Power Fx Example: Greeting in the User's Language

This short example illustrates Ask-a-question, variable setting, and a system
variable in one flow:

1. Add an **Ask a question** node: "What is your name?" Save the response as
   `user_name`.
2. Add a **Set variable** node. Use the expression:
Concat("Hello, ", Upper(Local.user_name), "! Your language is set to ",
System.User.Language, ".")

   Save the result as `greeting`.

3. Add a **Send message** node. In the message body, reference `{Local.greeting}`.

Running this workflow greets the user with their name in uppercase and echoes
their locale back to them. This is a trivial example, but it demonstrates how
local variables, system variables, and string functions compose cleanly.

## Managing Workflow Versions

Every time you save, Foundry creates a new, immutable version and appends it to
the version history. Open the **Version** dropdown to the left of the Save
button to browse past versions or delete ones you no longer need. You cannot
edit a past version in place; you can only view it and, if needed, delete it.

This versioning model fits naturally with a review process: developers build
and test changes in a draft workflow, then save a named version for stakeholders
to review before promoting it to production. If you are managing workflow YAML
in a Git repository (via the VS Code extensions), your Git history and Foundry's
version history will both carry a record of changes. Use one as the source of
truth and treat the other as a mirror.

The **YAML Visualizer View** toggle switches between the graphical canvas and the
raw YAML. The two representations are always in sync. If you prefer to author
workflow logic as text and use the canvas only for review, you can work
exclusively in YAML. This is particularly useful for complex branching logic
that is easier to read as indented YAML than as a web of arrows on a canvas.

## Troubleshooting Common Problems

**The Workflows menu is not visible, or you cannot create a workflow.**
You need at minimum the Contributor role on the Foundry project. Check your
Azure RBAC assignment. Reader-level access lets you view workflows but not
create or edit them.

**A node produces unexpected output.**
Inspect the run log for that node. The most common causes are: the agent node
has no agent assigned, the JSON schema is syntactically invalid, or an upstream
variable is empty because an earlier node failed silently.

**Power Fx formula error: "Name isn't valid".**
Add the `Local.` or `System.` scope prefix. Foundry does not infer scope
automatically.

**Power Fx formula error: "Type mismatch".**
A variable is being used as a type it is not. Use `Text()`, `Value()`, or
`Boolean()` to coerce explicitly, or trace back to where the variable was set
and confirm its type there.

**The workflow times out.**
Break large, deeply nested workflows into smaller sub-workflows connected by
agent calls. Check that any external HTTP calls made by agent tools have
reasonable timeouts. A tool that waits indefinitely on a slow API will stall
the entire workflow run.

## Summary

Workflows are the orchestration tier that sits above individual agents. They let
you coordinate multiple agents in a predictable order (sequential), route
dynamically between specialists (group chat), or pause for human input at any
point in the process (human in the loop). Power Fx provides the formula language
to express branching logic, transform variables, and route the flow without
dropping into code.

The most important design discipline with workflows is to resist the temptation
to push control-flow logic into agent prompts. Prompts are for language; the
workflow canvas is for logic. Keep them separate and your workflows will be
easier to test, debug, and audit.
